name: Planning fallacy
statement: People predict they will finish sooner than they do, and asking them for their worst case moves the estimate without making it more accurate.
meaning: Two literatures travel under the name and they measure different things. The psychological one asks individuals when they will finish a real task, then records when they actually finish. The finding is a gap in one direction: the prediction is early, the completion is late, and the person making the prediction is confident in it. Kahneman and Tversky's account is about which information gets used. Singular information concerns the case at hand, how this project will go. Distributional information concerns how long comparable projects took. Forecasters build a plausible scenario from the first and leave the second on the table, so the estimate describes a run in which nothing goes wrong. The second literature counts cost overruns on large infrastructure, where the same shape appears at organisational scale. Whether the two have the same cause is the open question, and the megaproject data are the reason it is open.

origin.where: TIMS Studies in the Management Sciences
origin.note: The standard citation is "Intuitive prediction: Biases and corrective procedures", volume 12, pages 313-327, which was not opened during this check. The same paper circulated two years earlier as Decision Research technical report PTR-1042-77-6, dated June 1977, and that version was read. It carries the phrase in quotation marks: "Although this 'planning fallacy' is sometimes attributable to motivational factors such as wishful thinking, it frequently occurs even when underestimation of duration or cost is actually penalized." It also sets out the singular and distributional distinction, and recommends the adoption of what it calls an 'external approach', which treats the specific problem as one of many.

evidence: Buehler, Griffin and Ross supplied the numbers everyone quotes, in five studies in 1994. Study 1 telephoned 37 psychology students in the final semester of the honours thesis course at the University of Waterloo and asked when they would submit. Four had still not submitted when the records closed two semesters later, so every figure below rests on the other 33. Their best estimate averaged 33.9 days; they took 55.5, t(32) = 3.43, p < .002. Fewer than a third, 29.7%, finished by the date they had named. Asked to assume everything went as badly as it possibly could, they said 48.6 days against the same 55.5, and the paper reports that remaining gap as not significant, t(32) = 1.03. Only 48.7% finished by that worst case. Predictions were informative despite the bias: predicted and actual times correlated at .77. Study 2 recruited 104 undergraduates to name one academic and one non-academic project they meant to finish within a week. Three could not be reached afterwards, and the means come from the 91 academic and 62 non-academic projects that were finished by the follow-up. Academic projects were predicted at 5.8 days and reported at 10.7, F(1, 87) = 20.00, non-academic at 5.0 and 9.2, F(1, 58) = 6.65, with 37.1% and 42.5% finished on time. Participants told outright that the researchers would compare their predictions against their completion times were no less optimistic than those who were not told. Study 4 gave 123 students a computer tutorial assignment whose finishing time the machine recorded without their knowledge. Its 41 controls predicted 5.5 days and took 6.8. The 40 students first made to describe past assignments and then to write a scenario connecting that history to this assignment predicted 7.0 days and took 7.0, and 60.0% of them finished within their prediction against 29.3% of controls. Study 5 turned the task over to strangers. Its 123 observers, three yoked to each of the 41 controls and given that person's details, deadline and self-prediction, forecast 8.5 days where the actors forecast 5.5 and the true figure was 6.8. The field counterpart is Flyvbjerg, Skamris Holm and Buhl's sample of 258 transportation infrastructure projects worth $90 billion, completed between 1927 and 1998 in 20 countries. Actual costs exceeded the estimate in 86% of them. Averaged across all 258 projects, including those that came in under, costs ran 27.6% above estimate: 44.7% for rail, 33.8% for bridges and tunnels and 20.4% for roads.

replication.headline: The finding holds where people predict their own real deadlines and dissolves elsewhere: observers overshoot, brief laboratory tasks show no bias or overestimation, and the megaproject overruns that made the idea famous have a rival explanation its own author prefers.
replication.detail: Searches of Crossref, PubMed and the open web found no registered or multi-site replication of the 1994 studies. What exists is a review, one recent preregistered field test, repeated demonstrations in the original paradigm, and field data that point the other way. Halkjelsvik and Jorgensen reviewed the judgment-based time-prediction literature across psychology, engineering and management. Underestimation was reported more often than overestimation in the engineering and management studies, and not in the psychology studies. They also question the recurring claim that small tasks are overestimated and large ones underestimated, on the grounds that random error alone can produce that pattern. Their own 2026 experiments on brief tasks with duration feedback found bias not discernible from zero in three of five studies and overestimation in the other two. The preregistered test is Gligoric, Piccardi, Hofman and West, who had students in an EPFL data-analysis course predict how long a replication exercise would take. Across the 329 students who completed all four surveys, of 354 enrolled, expected time averaged 9.01 hours against 10.53 taken, p = .0309, with 62% running over. Those authors never use the phrase planning fallacy and their completion times are self-reported. Roy, Christenfeld and McKenzie offer a different mechanism for the same data: people recall past episodes as shorter than they were, so an accurate use of memory still yields a short forecast. Griffin and Buehler replied in the same issue that the two accounts have different domains, and Roy and colleagues answered that both can hold at once. On the field side the record is contested. Love, Sing, Ika and Newton examined about HK$115 billion of Hong Kong transportation work. They report that 47% of projects deviated from their approved budget, with deviations running in both directions, and argue the planning fallacy does not describe how such projects behave. Chapman and Eliasson cover every Swedish road and rail investment finalised between 1998 and 2025, in a preprint. They report that 3% of roads and 6% of rail fit the planning fallacy pattern of missing on both cost and benefits. Half the roads, 52%, and 40% of the rail projects were plainly successful. Against that, the laboratory result survives the obvious deflationary reading. Buehler and colleagues' students had no reason to underbid, were told in one condition that their accuracy would be checked, and were still optimistic, and in Study 4 the completion time came off a computer log rather than self-report.

study.cite: Halkjelsvik, T., & Jorgensen, M. (2012). From origami to software development: A review of studies on judgment-based predictions of performance time. Psychological Bulletin, 138(2), 238-271.

limits: The two literatures should not be pooled, and most of the trouble with the idea comes from pooling them. Buehler and colleagues measured individuals predicting their own completion dates over days and weeks. Flyvbjerg measured organisations forecasting the cost of works costing hundreds of millions. Cost is not time and an institution is not a person. The full text of the 1994 paper was read for this check, and no standardised effect size appears anywhere in it. It reports means, t and F statistics, one chi-square and correlations, so the structured fields above are empty. Study 1's figures also flatter the students, because its four non-submitters are dropped from every mean and they had still not handed in two semesters after the survey. Study 2 relied on self-reported completion times, a limitation its authors name, and its means exclude the projects still unfinished at the follow-up. The 1979 chapter that gave the effect its name was not opened. Crossref and general web search produced no free copy, and Crossref records a reprint in Judgment under Uncertainty (1982) at pages 414-421 that is paywalled at Cambridge. Flyvbjerg's 2002 and 2006 papers were read in the author-accepted versions posted to arXiv rather than in the journals. Love and colleagues, Batselier and Vanhoucke and the Swedish preprint were read at abstract level only, and the Swedish study has not been peer reviewed. Duration is also the narrow case. Whether the same pull operates on estimates of cost, effort or difficulty for one person is not settled by the studies above.
misreadings: The most common error is to state the effect without the possessive. People underestimate their own completion times. In Study 5 observers handed the same information overshot, predicting 8.5 days against an actual 6.8, and their absolute error was no better than the actors', running 2.6 to 2.8 days across the three observer conditions against the actors' 1.8. Two groups wrong in opposite directions is not one bias. The second error is the worst-case remedy. Asking for a pessimistic estimate moved the mean from 33.9 days to 48.6, which still sat below the actual 55.5, though the paper reports that residual gap as not significant. Its absolute error, 23.2 days, was no smaller than the best guess's 22.6. What worked in Study 4 was narrower: recalling past assignments changed little on its own, and the correction came from being made to write out how this assignment would go if it went the way previous ones had. The third error is to treat the most retold story as data. Kahneman's account of his Israeli curriculum team appears in Thinking, Fast and Slow and is a memoir. The team's private estimates centred on two years, the curriculum expert then recalled that no comparable team had finished in under seven years and that about 40% had failed, and the book arrived eight years later and was never used. The fourth error is treating cost overruns on megaprojects as proof of a cognitive slip. Flyvbjerg, Skamris Holm and Buhl found no improvement in accuracy over time, with year of decision failing to predict the error at p = 0.22 on the 111 projects for which that date was available. They take that as evidence against appraisal optimism: a profession that never learns is implausible where a profession rewarded for underbidding is not. Their conclusion names strategic misrepresentation, which they gloss as lying. Flyvbjerg's later overview of biases in project management ranks strategic misrepresentation first and the planning fallacy fourth rather than choosing between them. His remedy is indifferent between them. Reference class forecasting replaces the forecaster's judgment with the distribution of outcomes from comparable finished projects, which routes around a liar and an optimist alike. The American Planning Association endorsed the method in April 2005. From August 2004 the UK Department for Transport required local authorities seeking funds to apply uplifts derived from it: 32% on a road scheme and 57% on a metro rail scheme, for anyone wanting an 80% chance of staying inside budget. Batselier and Vanhoucke report that on real project data the method beat both earned value management and Monte Carlo simulation for cost and for time.
